# Point

```{r}
#| include: false
source("../R/setup.R")
```

How does one measurement change as another changes? `point` draws one glyph,
a small symbol, at the `(x, y)` position of each row. The glyph is a dot unless
you choose another.

The plot it makes is the **scatterplot**, and it was invented later than the
other basic charts. William Playfair published the line chart and the bar chart
in 1786 [@playfair1786], and the pie chart in 1801 [@playfair1801]. The first
scatterplot came in 1833, about thirty years after the pie chart: historians
usually name John Herschel as the first person to plot one measured column
against another. He plotted the position of a double star against the year,
then drew a smooth curve through the dots so the trend could be seen
[@friendly2005]. Other names for the same
picture are scatter diagram and scattergram. When `size` maps a third column,
the same plot is called the bubble chart.

None of those chart names is a word in gog, and that is deliberate. `point`
is a **mark**, not a chart. `point + x(gdp) + y(life)` is a scatterplot,
and `point + x(continent) + y(life)` is a **strip plot**. The mark is the same in
both. The chart name belongs to the whole sentence, not to any word in the
vocabulary. That is why the names are listed in an appendix, [Chart
names](../chart-names.qmd), instead of in the kernel.

## Basic usage {#basic-usage}

Do people in richer countries live longer? The `gapminder_2007` table can
answer that. It holds one row per country in 2007, with the country's `gdp`,
its life expectancy `life`, its `continent` and its `population`. [The book's
data](../book-data.qmd) says where the table comes from. Most examples in this
chapter start from the smallest sentence that draws a point: the table, the
mark, and its two positions.

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gapminder_2007)
```

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life)
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life."*

Each dot is one row, one country, placed by its `gdp` and its `life`. Nothing
else about the row is shown yet. The answer to the opening question is yes:
life expectancy rises quickly with gdp among the poorer countries, then slowly
among the richer ones. Both columns hold numbers, so
each axis is a linear scale. Most of the dots are on the left, because most
countries have far lower incomes than the richest few. The
[Scales](../scales.qmd) chapter shows the log scale that spreads them out.

## The dot as a default {#the-dot-as-a-default}

Write `point` and you get a dot. Calling it *the dot mark* is accurate whenever
no `shape` is mapped or set. But the dot is only a *default*, and you can change it. A
point is *a glyph at a position*, and `shape` replaces the dot with one of the
seven glyphs gog draws, a different one for each category of a column. [Shape](#shape) below names the
seven, says which category gets which, and what to do with more than seven.

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + shape(continent) +
  title("The glyph is not always a dot")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, shape by continent."*

So "a dot" means the circle, the first of the seven glyphs, drawn when you name
no `shape`.

To draw every point with the same glyph instead, set one with `style()`. The
seven are `circle`, `square`, `triangle`, `diamond`, `cross`, `star` and `wye`,
and [Shape](#shape) draws each of them:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + style(shape = "triangle") +
  title("One glyph for every point")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, with shape triangle."*

The [`text`](text.qmd) mark is close to `point`. Both draw one symbol per row
at `(x, y)`, and they differ only in what that symbol is. A point draws one of
the seven glyphs, chosen with `shape`. A text mark draws the value of a column,
chosen with `label`. Put both on one plot and each row is
located by a dot and named by its label.

The `medals` table holds five countries, one row each, with the number of
`gold`, `silver` and `bronze` medals each country won:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(medals)
```

```{r}
data(medals) + point + style(size = 5, color = "#9e9e9e") +
  text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) + style(nudge = "up") +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("point and text on one plot")
```

*"Given the medals: points and also text, x is gold, y is silver, label by
country."*

The dot shows where each country is, and the label names it.
`style(nudge = "up")` moves each label above its dot, so the two do not cover
each other.

## A categorical x: the strip plot {#a-categorical-x-the-strip-plot}

Every plot so far has put a measurement on `x`, but `x` also accepts a
categorical column. Each category gets its own slot on the axis, and every row
is drawn in its category's slot. You see the whole distribution rather than a
summary of it:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(continent) + y(life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("One dot per country")
```

Every mark places a categorical column this way, `bar` included. Compare the
strip plot with `bar * mean`, which reduces each group to one number:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(continent) + y(life) +
  y_label("Mean life expectancy") + title("The same data, summarized")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by mean, x is continent, y is life."*

`mean` is not the bar's own transform. Other marks take it too, and each draws
the same means in its own way:

| Mark derived by `mean` | What it draws |
|---|---|
| `point * mean` | one dot at each mean |
| `line * mean` | the means joined into a profile |
| `area * mean` | the same profile, filled to the baseline |
| `step * mean` | each mean held flat until the next category |
| `bar * mean` | one bar per category, the plot above |

`median`, `sum`, `min` and `max` can replace `mean` in every row of that table.
So can `quantile`, which needs a probability: `quantile(0.9)` is the value nine
tenths of each group falls below.
The statistic decides the number, and the mark decides how it is drawn.

The strip plot shows Africa's spread and its overlap with Asia; the bar chart
shows neither. The strip plot has one weakness: every point in a category is
on the same vertical line. Where many countries have close values, their dots
cover each other, and you cannot see how many there are. There are four ways to
show the overlapping points.

The first way is to make each point partly transparent with one setting,
`style(opacity = 0.6)`, so overlap reads as a darker area. The horizontal strip
plot in [Either axis](#either-axis-a-horizontal-strip) below is drawn this way.
The second way is [`point *
jitter`](../transforms.qmd#jitter-spread-sideways-along-the-category). It moves
overlapping points sideways along the categorical axis, and never changes their
measured value:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point * jitter + x(continent) + y(life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("The same dots, spread sideways")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points derived by jitter, x is continent, y is life."*

Every dot keeps its life expectancy, so its height has not changed. Only its
place inside its continent's slot has changed, and that place means nothing:
the dot still reads as its continent. `jitter` moves a dot only along the
categorical axis, inside its slot, and never along the measured axis. By
default `jitter` moves a dot at most 0.2 of a slot from its category's center.
The number in `jitter()` multiplies that default, so `jitter(0.5)` spreads the
dots half as wide ([How much to
spread](../transforms.qmd#how-much-to-spread-jitteramount)). In a
scatterplot both axes are measurements, so a moved dot would show a value the
data does not hold. gog never draws a point at a value that was not measured,
not even to keep points from covering each other. So it refuses `point * jitter`
when `x` and `y` are both continuous, as [What it refuses](#what-it-refuses)
shows.

The third way,
[`point * dodge`](../transforms.qmd#dodge-side-by-side-instead-of-on-top), also
moves points sideways within their slot. Unlike `jitter`, it moves each point
only as far as it must to touch no other point:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point * dodge + x(continent) + y(life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("The same dots, set apart until none touch")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points derived by dodge, x is continent, y is life."*

With 142 countries, no dot covers another, and every dot keeps its life
expectancy. Where many
countries have close values, the dots spread wide, so the outline of each group
shows the shape of its distribution, one dot per country. This plot is the
**beeswarm** [@eklund2021beeswarm]. When a slot is too crowded to hold its dots, gog draws the extra
ones at the slot's edge, on top of one another, and a warning says how many
overlap. It never moves them into the next continent's slot. When a slot is
full, add `style(opacity = )` as well: the dots drawn over one another at the
slot's edge then show as a darker band, so you can see where they overlap.

The fourth way is to count the overlapping points instead of separating them.
[`point * bin * stack`](../transforms.qmd#the-dot-plot) cuts the measured
column into bins and piles one dot per row above each bin, which is the
**dot plot** [@wilkinson1999dotplots]. It shows one distribution, with the measure on `x`;
`| facet(continent)` draws one for each continent. The cookbook draws it with [thirty
rows](../cookbook/one-variable.qmd#when-there-are-only-thirty-rows), where every
row is still visible. Choose among the four ways by what you want the reader
to see. Opacity, `jitter` and `dodge` keep the spread: on the measured axis, every
dot stays where its value was measured. Opacity leaves every dot in its place, and with `dodge`
no dot covers another unless its slot is full. `bin * stack` gives the count: how many rows fall in each bin. The result looks like a bar chart, but
each row is still its own dot.

### Either axis: a horizontal strip {#either-axis-a-horizontal-strip}

gog decides a plot's direction from which axis holds which column: the axis
that carries the category sets it, for a point exactly as for a
[bar](bar.qmd#horizontal-bars). So the category can be on `y` instead of `x`,
and the strips run horizontally. The countries and the distributions are the
same, and each continent's dots now run from left to right:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(life) + y(continent) +
  style(opacity = 0.6) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same distributions, lying down")
```

If you know ggplot2's `coord_flip()`, there is no such word here. Swapping the
columns on `x` and `y` was the whole change, the same way you swap the two arguments of
matplotlib's `scatter()`. Use the horizontal form when the category names are
too long for the bottom axis. It also helps when there are many categories,
since names listed down the left side are easier to read than names crowded
along the bottom.

The same holds for the ways of setting dots apart: with the category on `y`,
`point * jitter` and `point * dodge` spread the dots up and down instead of
sideways. Here is the beeswarm lying down:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point * dodge + x(life) + y(continent) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The beeswarm, lying down")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points derived by dodge, x is life, y is continent."*

With one row per category, the horizontal strip is the **Cleveland dot plot**
[@cleveland1984].
It shares a name with the dot plot above but is a different chart: there each
dot is one row in a bin, and here each dot is one category's value. [Comparing
categories](../cookbook/comparing.qmd#what-if-the-differences-are-small) draws
it for twelve countries.

A point derived by `count` can be horizontal too.
[`point * count`](../transforms.qmd#count-frequency-aggregation) counts the rows
in each category and draws one point for each. With the category on `y`, that
is a Cleveland dot plot of the counts:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point * count + y(continent) + x_label("Countries") +
  title("How many countries each continent holds")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points derived by count, y is continent."*

Africa holds the most countries, 52, and Oceania the fewest, 2. Three other
transforms also compute a number from the one column you name. `bin` counts the
rows in each range of a measured column, and `proportion` gives each category's
share of the rows. `density` estimates, as a smooth curve, where a measured
column's values are most common. On a point, as on a bar, the computed number goes on the axis you
left empty. Name the column on `y`, and the count, share or density is drawn
along `x`.

## Color {#color}

In the scatterplot of `gdp` against `life`, every dot looks the same, so you
cannot see which continent each country is in. Bind `color` to a categorical
column to color points by group. gog assigns a distinct color from a 20-color
palette automatically.

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  color(continent)
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, color by continent."*

Most African countries are at the lower left, and most European countries at
the upper right. gog adds a color legend whenever you map a column to `color`.

### Splitting without color {#splitting-points-without-color}

Sometimes another layer already uses color, such as boxes colored by era. The
points should then be split the same way without being painted. `color` does two
things at once: it splits the points into groups, and it paints each group.
[`group`](../channels.qmd#group) does only the first. On points with no
statistic and no `dodge`, splitting changes nothing, because each row is already
its own point, and gog refuses it ([What it refuses](#what-it-refuses)). With
`dodge` or a statistic, `group` decides which rows go together, and the other
layer shows the colors. The `gm_eras` table holds each country's life expectancy
in 1957 and in 2007:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gm_eras)
```

Here the boxes are colored by era, and `point * dodge` draws one dot per row,
so each country appears twice, once for each era. `group(era)` gives each era
its own half of the continent's slot, as `dodge` does for the boxes, so each
era's dots are drawn over that era's box:

```{r}
data(gm_eras) + box * dodge + color(era) +
  point * dodge + group(era) + style(size = 2.5) +
  x(continent) + y(life)
```

*"Given the gapminder eras: boxes derived by dodge, colored by era, and also
points derived by dodge, grouped by era, with size 2.5, x is continent, y is
life."*

Without `group(era)`, each continent's dots would form one beeswarm in the
middle of its slot, between its two boxes. `style(size = 2.5)` draws smaller
dots, so more of them fit in each half of a crowded slot.

A statistic is split the same way. `point * mean + group(era)` computes one
mean for each era within each continent. Here colored lines join each era's
means across the continents, and black dots mark the means themselves:

```{r}
data(gm_eras) + line * mean + color(era) +
  point * mean + group(era) + style(color = "black") +
  x(continent) + y(life)
```

*"Given the gapminder eras: lines derived by mean, colored by era, and also
points derived by mean, grouped by era, colored black, x is continent, y is
life."*

Without `group(era)`, `point * mean` would compute one mean for each continent
from both eras, and each dot would be between the two lines.

## Shape {#shape}

Which glyph does each category get, and what happens when there are more
categories than glyphs? `shape` maps a categorical column to one of seven
glyphs. In order, they are the circle, the square, the triangle, the diamond,
the cross, the star and the wye, which looks like the letter Y. The categories
are ordered by where each first appears in the table, or by the
[order you declare](../data.qmd#declaring-the-order-of-categories). The first
category gets the circle, the second the square, and so on. Here is the whole
set, in the order gog assigns them:

```{r}
glyphs <- data.frame(
  glyph = c("circle", "square", "triangle", "diamond", "cross", "star", "wye"),
  row   = c(1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1)
)
data(glyphs) + point + x(glyph) + y(row) + shape(glyph) +
  style(size = 8) + x_label("") + y_label("") +
  title("The seven glyphs, in the order they are assigned")
```

*"Given the glyphs table: points, x is glyph, y is row, shape by glyph, with
size 8."*

Asia comes first in the gapminder table, so Asia is the circle, and every
continent legend in this chapter lists Asia first. Seven is the whole set gog
draws. Map
`shape` to a column with more than seven categories and the eighth category
gets the circle again, so two categories share a glyph and look the same. gog says so when
that happens, naming the number of categories and the seven glyphs, and the plot still draws. The
`nutrients` table has eight foods, one more than there are glyphs:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(nutrients)
```

```{r}
#| message: true
data(nutrients) + point + x(nutrient) + y(amount) + shape(food) +
  y_label("Amount per 100g") + title("Eight foods, seven glyphs")
```

*"Given the nutrients: points, x is nutrient, y is amount, shape by food."*

Oats is the eighth food in the table, so its points are circles, the glyph
salmon already has. Nothing in the picture shows which circles are salmon and
which are oats, so the message counts the foods and the glyphs for you. The book
has four ways to draw more than seven groups:

- `color`, whose default palette has 20 colors, as [Color](#color) above
  does with the continents.
- One panel per category with `facet`, folded into rows so the panels stay
  wide: [Folding a long line of
  panels](../faceting.qmd#folding-a-long-line-of-panels).
- The name on the point instead of a glyph: a `text` layer with `label`, the
  [labeled scatter](text.qmd#both-at-once-the-labeled-scatter), and
  [`repel`](text.qmd#repel-moving-labels-off-each-other) when the names
  overlap. Of the four, only this one can name each of a hundred categories.
  In the web edition, a
  [brush](../selection.qmd#which-one-is-that) dims the labels outside the
  selection, so only the selected names stay readable. A `text` layer that
  uses `repel` is not dimmed: the brush leaves its labels as they are.
- Every category in one pale color, and the few that matter drawn again on
  top, in a second layer: [What settings are
  for](../style.qmd#what-settings-are-for).

When a table has two categorical columns, map `shape` to the one with fewer
categories. `continent` has five, and seven glyphs are enough for five.
`country` has 142, so it goes on a label or a facet instead.

Some readers cannot see the difference between colors, and a black-and-white
printout removes it. Map `color` and `shape` to the same column, and the glyphs
still separate the groups:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  color(continent) + shape(continent)
```

Each continent now differs in two ways, so either one alone still separates the
groups.

## Size {#size}

Once `x` and `y` are both bound, no position is free for a third measurement.
The `size` channel can show it instead. `size` maps a continuous column to the
point's radius, from 3 pixels at the smallest value to 12 at the largest.

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  color(continent) + size(population)
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, color by continent, size by
population."*

The two largest dots are China and India, and both are at the left, among the
poorer countries. gog adds a size legend showing the column's minimum,
maximum, and the value halfway between them.

Two transforms in a chain can supply the number on `y` and the number on `size`.
The `count` transform counts each continent's rows and writes the result to a
column named `count`. The
[`cumulative`](../transforms.qmd#cumulative-the-running-total) transform then
adds each continent's count to the counts before it, and the point is drawn at
that running total. The `count` column still holds each continent's own count,
so `size(count)` can show it:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point * count * cumulative + x(continent) + size(count) +
  title("Running count of countries, sized by each continent's count")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points derived by count and cumulative, x is continent,
size by count."*

The last point is at 142, every country in the table. Africa's point is the
largest, because Africa adds 52 countries, the most of any continent. Oceania's
point is the smallest: it adds only 2 to the total.

## Opacity {#opacity}

`opacity` is a setting, as the [horizontal strip plot](#either-axis-a-horizontal-strip) above showed, and it is
also a channel: a larger value in a continuous column gives a more opaque point.
Population is skewed, so a linear scale would leave China and India dark and
the rest faint. The log scale spreads the values across the range:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  opacity(population, scale = "log") +
  title("Opacity: population, on a log scale")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, opacity by population on a
log scale."*

See [Channels and legends](../channels.qmd) for the range of opacities a mapped column uses and why `line`
does not accept this channel.

That example maps opacity to a column. Often there is no column to show: the
only problem is that many points overlap. Then you want one opacity on every
point instead. That is a *setting* rather than a mapping, so you write
`style(opacity = )` and no legend appears; see [Setting vs
mapping](../style.qmd). The `gm_all` table holds every gapminder country in
every year, so the points overlap heavily:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gm_all)
```

```{r}
data(gm_all) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  style(opacity = 0.2, size = 3) +
  title("Every point at one opacity")
```

*"Given all the gapminder years: points, x is gdp, y is life, with opacity
0.2."*

Where many points overlap, the color is darker, and the darkest area is at the
left, where most countries were in most years. A hollow point is the other way
to show the same crowding, and [What you can set](#what-you-can-set) draws this
table with it.

## All channels at once {#all-channels-at-once}

A table often has more columns to show than two positions can hold. The
`color`, `shape` and `size` channels can show the others, and all three can be
on one plot at once. Here
`continent` is mapped to both `color` and `shape`, so the groups stay separate
in black-and-white printing, and `population` is mapped to `size`:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  color(continent) +
  shape(continent) +
  size(population) +
  title("GDP, life expectancy, and population")
```

Four columns now show in one picture: `gdp` and `life` by position, `continent`
by color and glyph, and `population` by size.

## Transforms it takes {#transforms-it-takes}

A transform computes new values from the rows, and the mark draws those values
instead of the rows. The table lists, by kind, the transforms a point takes and
the ones it refuses:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
mark_transforms("point")
```

The plots below show every transform a point takes. Within a figure the plots
differ mainly in their transform, and the paragraph before each figure names any
other change.

**Counting.** `count` and `proportion` tally the rows at each value of `x`, on a
category or a number. `bin` and `density` work on a number. `bin` counts the
rows in each interval, and `density` estimates, as a smooth curve, how closely
the rows lie along the axis. Each puts its result on the axis you leave empty.
The top two plots put `continent` on `x`, and the bottom two put `life`. The
curve is computed at 256 places unless you set `places`, and 256 dots would
touch and look like a line, so the last plot asks for 32:

```{r}
((data(gapminder_2007) + point * count + x(continent) + title("point * count")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point * proportion + x(continent) +
     title("point * proportion"))) /
  ((data(gapminder_2007) + point * bin + x(life) + title("point * bin")) |
     (data(gapminder_2007) + point * density(places = 32) + x(life) +
        title("point * density(places = 32)")))
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points derived by count, x is continent, beside points
derived by proportion, x is continent; above points derived by bin, x is life,
beside points derived by density at 32 places, x is life."*

**Summaries.** The six summaries reduce the rows at each value of `x` to one
value, so they need a number on `y`. `sum` reads `population`, because only an
amount has a total that means something. The other five read `life`. They give
the mean, the median, the largest and the smallest value, and `quantile(0.9)`
gives the value that nine tenths of the rows fall below:

```{r}
((data(gapminder_2007) + point * sum + x(continent) + y(population) +
    title("point * sum")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point * mean + x(continent) + y(life) +
     title("point * mean")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point * median + x(continent) + y(life) +
     title("point * median"))) /
  ((data(gapminder_2007) + point * max + x(continent) + y(life) +
      title("point * max")) |
     (data(gapminder_2007) + point * min + x(continent) + y(life) +
        title("point * min")) |
     (data(gapminder_2007) + point * quantile(0.9) + x(continent) + y(life) +
        title("point * quantile(0.9)")))
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points derived by sum, x is continent, y is population,
beside points derived by mean, x is continent, y is life, beside points derived
by median, x is continent, y is life; above points derived by max, x is
continent, y is life, beside points derived by min, x is continent, y is life,
beside points derived by quantile at 0.9, x is continent, y is life."*

The five plots that read `life` share one scale, so their heights can be
compared from plot to plot.

**Fitted lines.** `smooth` and `straight` need a number on each axis. They fit a
line to the rows, each placed at its `x` and its `y`. `smooth` follows the
shape of the data, and `straight` is the least-squares line. A point draws each
fitted line as dots at evenly spaced places along `x`: 100 of them, unless you
set `places`. The first two plots ask for 24, so that each dot can be
seen.

**Running total.** `cumulative` adds each value to the ones before it along the
axis. The third plot reads the `actuals` table, with `year` on `x` and `sales`
on `y`. The table holds one year of sales in each row:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(actuals)
```

```{r}
(data(gapminder_2007) + point * smooth(places = 24) + x(gdp) + y(life) +
   title("point * smooth(places = 24)")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point * straight(places = 24) + x(gdp) + y(life) +
     title("point * straight(places = 24)")) |
  (data(actuals) + point * cumulative + x(year) + y(sales) +
     title("point * cumulative"))
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points derived by smooth at 24 places, x is gdp, y is
life, beside points derived by straight at 24 places, x is gdp, y is life;
beside points from the actuals,
derived by cumulative, x is year, y is sales."*

**Collision modifiers.** Collision modifiers move marks that would be drawn on
top of one another. `dodge` moves each point
just far enough to touch no other point, and `jitter` moves each point a short
way along the category axis. Both need a category on one axis. `stack` piles one
dot for each row, so on a point it needs `bin` or `count` written before it, to
group the rows. The result is the dot plot, with `life` on `x` and no `y`. The
dots are drawn smaller here, with `style(size = 2.5)`, because two plots share
the width, so each continent's slot is narrow:

```{r}
(((data(gapminder_2007) + point * dodge + x(continent) + y(life) +
     style(size = 2.5) + title("point * dodge")) |
    (data(gapminder_2007) + point * jitter + x(continent) + y(life) +
       style(size = 2.5) + title("point * jitter"))) /
   (data(gapminder_2007) + point * bin * stack + x(life) + style(size = 2.5) +
      title("point * bin * stack"))) +
  theme(height = 800)
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points derived by dodge, x is continent, y is life,
beside points derived by jitter, x is continent, y is life; above points derived
by bin and stack, x is life."*

**Layouts.** `layout` places the names in an **edge table** (one row for each
link between two names) as a network. It needs two columns of names and the
network space, `network()`. A point draws each name as a dot at its place, and
`edge` draws the lines between them, as the [Edge](edge.qmd) chapter shows. The
`trade_partners` table holds one row for each pair of countries that trade, with
the exporter and the importer:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(trade_partners)
```

```{r}
data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(exporter, importer) +
  point * layout(exporter, importer) + network() +
  title("point * layout, with the edges")
```

*"Given trade partners: edges derived by layout from exporter to importer, and
also points derived by layout from exporter to importer, in the network."*

A point refuses every transform in the Refuses column above. The pair transforms
give `y` a low and a high at each value of `x`, which [`interval`](interval.qmd),
[`ribbon`](ribbon.qmd), `line` and `step` take. `partition`, `flow` and `cluster` lay out
rectangles, bands and branches, which [`zone`](zone.qmd), `ribbon` and
[`path`](path.qmd) draw. `repel` moves [`text`](text.qmd) labels off each other.

## What you can set {#what-you-can-set}

A setting changes how every point looks without reading a column, and each
mark takes its own. These are a point's settings, with the values each accepts:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
mark_options("point")
```

A point takes six settings, and it is the only mark that can set `shape`.
Every glyph except the cross is filled with color, so a point is also one of
the marks that draw a border. `size` is the radius in pixels, and
`border_color` and `border_size` give that border its own color and width.

A point layer can take several settings at once:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  style(shape = "diamond", size = 7, color = "steelblue",
        border_color = "navy", border_size = 1.5) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("A shape, a size, and a border")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, colored steelblue, with
shape diamond, size 7, border color navy and border size 1.5."*

Where two diamonds overlap, the navy border shows where one ends and the next
begins. That is what a border is for where many points crowd together. A `cross` has
no fill to outline, so `border_color` and `border_size` change nothing on that
glyph.

A border can also be the whole point. Set the fill color to `"none"` and give
the border a color, and each point is drawn hollow: an outline with no fill. A
hollow point can be partly transparent as well. `opacity` fades what `color`
paints, and `color = "none"` paints nothing, so gog refuses `opacity` on a
hollow point. Put the transparency in the border's color instead. In
`"#4682b44d"`, the first six hex digits are steelblue, and the last
two, `4d`, make the outline 30% opaque. Here are all 1,704 rows of `gm_all`
again, the table the [Opacity](#opacity) section drew at one opacity:

```{r}
data(gm_all) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  style(color = "none", border_color = "#4682b44d", size = 3) +
  title("Every point hollow, its outline partly transparent")
```

Where hollow points overlap, every outline stays visible, and where many pile
up, the outlines add up to a darker area. The plot shows each point and the
crowding at once. Neither this nor opacity moves a point off its measured value,
which is why they, and not `jitter`, are the answers for a crowded scatterplot. On a categorical axis,
`jitter` and `dodge` move points apart instead, as the [strip
plot](#a-categorical-x-the-strip-plot) showed.

`pattern` is not on the list. A hatch needs a large area and a dash needs a
long stroke, and a glyph is too small for either. To separate groups by glyph,
a point uses `shape` instead, and [What it refuses](#what-it-refuses) shows the
refusal.

The [grid of every mark and every setting](../style.qmd#what-you-can-set) shows
which other marks share this list. What a mark *maps* rather than sets is its
row on the [grid of marks and channels](../combinations.qmd#marks-and-channels).

## What it refuses {#what-it-refuses}

Five refusals follow, each with its reason: a category on `size`, any pattern,
`jitter` or `dodge` on a scatterplot, `opacity` on a hollow point, and `group`
on points with no statistic and no `dodge`.

`size` shows an amount, so it needs a column of amounts:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + size(continent)
```

Continents are names, not amounts, and a larger dot would claim an order the
data does not have. The message suggests `color` or `shape` instead: each
continent gets its own color or glyph.

The second refusal is about texture. A pattern is a dash along a stroke or a
hatch across an area, and a glyph is too small for either:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + style(pattern = "dashed")
```

The message names `shape`, which chooses a point's glyph.

The third refusal is `jitter` on a scatterplot. In a strip plot, `jitter` moves
a dot sideways inside its continent's slot. A place inside a slot has no scale,
so the move changes nothing a reader could measure. In a scatterplot both axes
are measurements, and every place on them is a value. A jittered dot would be drawn
at a gdp and a life expectancy that are not in the table. Two countries with the
same values would no longer look the same, and a reader who reads a dot against
the axes would read a number that was never measured. So gog refuses:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + point * jitter + x(gdp) + y(life)
```

This is a design rule, not a missing feature. Every dot is drawn at the values
in its row. gog never draws a point at a value that was not measured, not even
to keep points from covering each other, so `jitter` never moves a dot along a
measured axis. ggplot2's `geom_jitter()` moves points along both axes by a small
random amount, and gog does not. To show overlapping points in a
scatterplot, keep every point at its value and change how it is drawn.
`style(opacity = )`, which the message suggests, makes overlap read as a darker
area, as in the plot of every gapminder year under [Opacity](#opacity). A
hollow point, an outline with no fill, keeps every point visible where points
overlap, as the same table shows under [What you can set](#what-you-can-set).

`point * dodge` is refused on a scatterplot for the same reason. It moves a dot
only across a category's slot, and a scatterplot has no slot:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + point * dodge + x(gdp) + y(life)
```

The message again suggests `style(opacity = )`.

The fourth refusal is `opacity` on a hollow point. `opacity` fades what `color`
paints, and `color = "none"` paints nothing, so there is nothing for it to fade:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  style(color = "none", border_color = "steelblue", opacity = 0.3)
```

The message suggests `border_color = "#4682b44d"` instead. In `"#4682b44d"` the
transparency is part of the border's own color, as in the hollow points under
[What you can set](#what-you-can-set).

The fifth refusal is `group` on points with no statistic and no `dodge`. On a `line`,
`group` cuts one stroke into several. Points are not joined into a stroke, and
each row is already its own point, so splitting the rows by continent would
change nothing:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + group(continent)
```

gog accepts `group` on points only when a statistic or `dodge` is joined to
them, as in [Splitting without color](#splitting-points-without-color). A scatterplot
has no category axis for `dodge` to use, so the message offers the two channels
that show the groups: map `continent` to `color` or `shape` instead.

## In short {#in-short}

A point is a glyph at a position. The `point` mark draws one per row, unless a
transform such as `mean` summarizes the rows first. It is the only mark that maps `shape`, because
it is the only mark that picks its glyph from a fixed set. There are seven
glyphs, and an eighth category gets the circle again.

## What comes next {#what-comes-next}

The `point` mark draws each row as a separate glyph, and nothing joins one row
to the next. When one column puts the rows in order, such as years, the change
from one value to the next often matters most. [Line](line.qmd) joins the rows into one
stroke that shows whether the value rose or fell.
